newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: One year later, memories linger of Sri Lanka bomb.
newsitem.headline: One year later, memories linger of Sri Lanka bomb.

text.p: Colombo residents are trickling back into the capital's financial district nearly a year after a bomb destroyed Sri Lanka's Central Bank and killed 100 people, but fear still lingers.

A suspected Tamil separatist guerrilla rammed a lorry packed with what police said was a 500-kg (1,100-lb) plastic bomb into the Central Bank building on January 31 last year. The explosion brought down up a huge section of the nine-story building and killed 100 people, most of them office workers. About 1,400 other people were wounded.
"Soon after the bombing, there was this fear with people shunning the city centre," said Chandra Mohotti, general manager of the Galadari Hotel near the Central Bank.
"There was a big drop in activity in the downtown area which affected all the businesses. But we see it's slowly returning to normal. People are coming back," Mohotti told Reuters.
With the war now confined to remote areas in the island's north and east, Colombo's central district is back to normal.
But terrible memories remain.

"I saw a tiny red speck enlarge into a huge ball of yellow and white, all in a matter of seconds. Then I crashed to the floor," said Scott Dirckze, chairman of tea traders George Steuart and Company. He was in his eighth-floor office.
The buildings of several top Sri Lankan firms were badly damaged and for days, fires spewed black smoke into the air.
Four employees of George Steuart were killed and eight were blinded, totally or partially, by flying shards of glass. Many others were wounded.
"Every now and then I pick out tiny specks of glass from my forehead," Dirckze said.
Forty-one Central Bank employees were killed and some 230 were injured.

"I escaped without any injuries, but for the rest of the day I kept hearing of the deaths of so many of my co-workers," said a senior bank official who asked not to be named. "I could not believe it."
Six months after the bank bombing, suspected Tamil guerrillas exploded two bombs in a packed commuter train in a Colombo suburb, killing 57 people and injuring more than 500.
The Liberation Tigers of Tamil Ealam (LTTE), fighting for an independent state for minority Tamils in predominantly Sinhalese Sri Lanka, has not claimed responsibility for those bombings.
The government says more than 50,000 people have been killed in the 14-year-old conflict. The rebels say the number is higher, and that a majority of them were Tamils.

A month before the bank bombing, government troops forced the LTTE out of its stronghold in the northern Jaffna peninsula. The bombing, apparently in revenge for the Jaffna offensive, also disproved the goverment's claim that the LTTE was a spent force.
Last July, the LTTE overran a key army base on northeast coast, killing or capturing the camp's 1,000 men and dealing the military its worst blow of the war.

Earlier this month, the rebels again attacked a military base at Paranthan, a key road junction town south of Jaffna. The army said 223 soldiers were killed and the rebels said they lost at least 140.
The LTTE attack was repulsed, but there appeared to be no end in sight to the civil war.

President Chandrika Kuramatunga's government had proposed ending the war by "devolution" -- granting Tamils limited autonomy. But after the bombing, the plan met stiff opposition from Sinhalese hardliners who said it took too much power from the central government and rewarded separatism.
Now, a year after the bombing, government officials say their devolution proposals are alive and a final proposal for a referendum to amend the constitution will come in March.
But Kumaratunga needs the support of the opposition United National Party to push the plan through parliament, and insiders say bickering between the two parties may delay the proposal.
Also, the LTTE has given no sign it will back down from its demand for a separate state.
